body: One of the problems with filter_var is that it allows emails that you usually would not like to accept as valid form a form, for example "hello@local" is completely valid.

CakeEmail was switched to use filter_var entirely because it is far more permissive. People frequently use emails like `root@localhost` from cron jobs for error reporting. However, this is generally not an acceptable email address for account signups for example.

I don't think we should switch `Validation::email()` around personally.

OK. But then Validation::email() should not accept emails that are not valid with the default CakeMail::_validateEmail(). As is with the case user entering emails with Umlauts (e.g. üöäß) in the local part of the email address. 
In cakephp 2.4.9 CakeMail used the Validation::email method.

Maybe we can remove the umlauts in the front part of the email then again. If those are really invalid.

```
'/^[\p{L}0-9!#$%&\'*+\/=?^_`{|}~-]...
```

to

```
'/^[A-Z0-9!#$%&\'*+\/=?^_`{|}~-]...
```

Well I'm not so sure they are technically invalid either, because the local part of an email address should be up to the receiving mailserver to interpret. But filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) rejects them as invalid. And for what it's worth I can't create an email address with umlauts with my provider. 

So I think not allowing Umlauts in Validation::email is a good idea.
I think updating the `Vaildation::email()` regexp makes sense here then. However, there were tests added by @dereuromark in ed2054f4f to support unicode email addresses including ä and ö.

Yes, I was under the assumption that not only the domain but also the user part of the email could be utf8. An official document stating that only A-Z is allowed would be good. Especially in regards of future changes here that are possible (which would revert the revert) - they seem to allow more and more in domains/emails etc.

You can always further limit the validation in user land code.
But maybe the core code should be as allowing as possible.
I wish there was an official document. You have to comb through the various RFC's to figure out what is and is not valid sadly.

Hm looking at wikipedia it looks like the newer RFC 6530 permits unicode characters, the older RFC 5322 is still in use at many providers though. So I guess this could be viewed as a bug in php's ($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL).
see php tickets https://bugs.php.net/bug.php?id=65385 and https://bugs.php.net/bug.php?id=65630 and https://bugs.php.net/bug.php?id=65027
Using `idn_to_ascii` is tricky as it didn't exist before 5.3.0. We could conditionally use it if exists, and fallback to `urlencode()`.

I think using idn_to_ascii also only solves the domain part not the local part before the @. 

So far: php filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) is more permissive than Validate::email except that it doesn't allow for utf-8 email addresses. Validate::email allows for utf-8 but does not allow for emails such as user@localhost. 

To me it seems it would be best to not use php filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) in CakeMail::_validateEmail() but use a version of the Validate::email() regex except not checking for a TLD at the end. 

Then Validate::email and CakeMail::_validateEmail would behave more consistently, the front-end not allowing such emails as user@localhost, but still allowing newer utf-8 emails.
Note: we'll want to specify how this is different from the `filter_var` and why we made that decision, so as to avoid complaints in the future. Unsure if this is already the case.

Using `idn_to_ascii()` might work if both the local and domain were run through the function separately. I'm ok with using a more lax pattern though, no amount of validation will actually ensure delivery anyways. The validation was always intended to prevent developer error.

issue.title: Email Address Validation issue and SmtpTransport issue

repository.name: cakephp
repository.description: CakePHP: The Rapid Development Framework for PHP - Official Repository

issue.body:
This is a (multiple allowed):
- [x] bug
- [ ] enhancement
- [ ] feature-discussion (RFC)
### Versions
- CakePHP Version: 2.8.0
- MTA used: Exim version 4.86 (currently latest version)
### Issues

Two related issues:
- CakePHP's email validation allows non-ASCII letter characters, e.g. á, in the  local part of the email address (by the \p{L} unicode category construct in https://github.com/cakephp/cakephp/blob/2.8.0/lib/Cake/Utility/Validation.php#L472). This should not be allowed, see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_address#Local_part, or is at least highly impractical since SMTPUTF8 is not universally or even widely implemented, see e.g. "Just don't try to encode local parts." in https://lists.exim.org/lurker/message/20150424.200939.83d6ec81.en.html. Exim will reject the address.
- It also allows non-ASCII letter characters in the domain part. This allows Internationalized Domain Names (IDN). The problem here lies in the fact that this is not supported by the SmtpTransport. An SMTP client should convert them to so called punycode ASCII, according to https://lists.exim.org/lurker/message/20140812.120609.bf764769.en.html. Exim does not accept the SMTP sequence. By the way, conversion to punycode can be done by PHP's idn_to_ascii() (PHP 5 >= 5.3.0).
  This issues have been tested in the current 2.8 branch, but a quick code inspection confirms that they are also present in the master branch. As a workaround I have switched back to validation by PHP's filter_var(), used in a wrapper validation method.

The first issue can be fixed easily, although the right (i.m.h.o. almost universally implemented) RFCs may have to be consulted. For the second issue, if decided to support IDN for email, support it (maybe not only in the SmtpTransport).
### Also See
- https://github.com/cakephp/cakephp/issues/3742
- https://github.com/cakephp/cakephp/pull/3840
